prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

See, now You are finally offstage where we can talk. I can’t see through the drapes and pulleys, it’s too dark for me to turn them into moss and oaks, too dark for me to blink wooden risers into a bayou beautiful in near collapse that once ran a monstrous river into the Gulf, a scorched stew powerful only in sufficient stillness. No monstrance, no milagro, no brown scapular scraps, not even a woven palm frond. Just You and me. Just me, actually, standing with hip cocked and three fingers resting on my chin. Not even a naked household goddess above my bed where I ache and ache. I hate the Greeks, those bastards, for figuring You into some kind of flesh—though that cure is just a start. And the Romans tried, but flesh must do more than die: it has to live. And here’s what’s next. Me talking to You in Your most present absence, without even an apophatic clue. I imagine Your holy knees gathered to Your chin and Your arms bound twice around your legs. I imagine Your heart in a corner beating while You listen to my footfalls circle from the best damn hiding place of all.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker confronts a divine presence offstage, stripped of religious symbols, scenery, and ritual.
- The encounter feels profoundly solitary, as the speaker recognizes that they may actually be speaking only to themselves.
- The speaker rejects classical attempts to embody the divine in flesh because flesh must not merely die but also fully live.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker confronts an absent, hidden God beyond religious symbols and theatrical illusions, using intimate, bodily imagination and direct address to search for a divine presence that truly lives. This imagined encounter reveals absence itself as God’s most powerful hiding place, making the speaker’s restless longing and embodied attention a form of faith.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: See, You, Gulf

outputs.L1:
See, now You are finally offstage, where we can talk. And the Romans tried, but flesh must do more than die: it has to live.

And here’s what comes next: me talking to You in Your most present absence, without even an apophatic clue. I imagine Your holy knees drawn to Your chin, Your arms wrapped twice around Your legs. I imagine Your heart beating in a corner while You listen to my footfalls circling from the best damn hiding place of all.
outputs.L2: Look—you’re at last behind the scenes, somewhere we can speak. The curtains and rigging block my sight, and the darkness is too deep for me to remake them as oak trees and moss, or to transform the wooden platforms with a blink into a bayou, lovely in its near ruin, that once carried an immense river toward the Gulf—a burned, simmering mixture whose strength emerged only when it grew still enough. There is no sacred vessel, no miracle charm, no fragment of a brown scapular, not so much as a braided palm leaf. There is only You and me. In truth, there is only me, one hip tilted, three fingertips against my chin. Above the bed where I hurt without end, there is not even an unclothed domestic deity. I despise those Greek bastards for giving You a body, although that remedy goes only so far. The Romans made their attempt too, but a body cannot merely perish; it must also be alive. So this is the next step: I address You inside the absence where You feel most immediate, with no guidance even from negative theology. I picture Your sacred knees pulled up beneath Your chin, Your arms wrapped twice around Your legs. I picture Your heart beating in some corner as You hear my footsteps circling You while You remain concealed in the finest hiding place imaginable.
outputs.L3:
The speaker confronts a divine presence offstage, in a space stripped of religious symbols, scenery, and ritual. Nothing visible confirms that God is there, and the encounter is therefore marked by profound solitude. As the speaker continues, they begin to recognize that the voice they address may be no more than an echo of their own—that, in speaking to God, they may ultimately be speaking only to themselves.

This uncertainty also shapes the speaker’s rejection of classical attempts to embody the divine in human flesh. Such representations are inadequate because flesh cannot be defined solely by its mortality: it must not merely die, but also fully live, experiencing vulnerability, desire, pain, and change. Instead of relying on traditional theological images or doctrines, the speaker addresses God as a “present absence”—a presence sensed through its very invisibility. There is no certainty that God exists, and no stable language with which to name or describe the divine.

Yet the speaker continues to imagine God in intimate, bodily terms: hidden nearby, curled into a vulnerable posture, silent and watchful. God does not answer or reveal himself but listens as the speaker circles around him. The scene thus becomes less a conventional act of prayer than a tense encounter with silence, absence, and the speaker’s own need to believe that someone—or something—is listening.
outputs.L4:
The speaker addresses God not as a secure or familiar presence but as someone absent, concealed, and impossible to contain within conventional religious forms. Sacred symbols, rituals, and images may point toward the divine, yet they can also seem like theatrical devices: masks, costumes, and staged effects that create the appearance of presence without proving that anything living stands behind them. Refusing to be satisfied by such representations, the speaker turns directly toward the hidden God. The address is intimate and urgent, replacing distant theology with the language of the body, desire, touch, breath, and physical nearness. Through imagination, the speaker tries to bring God close enough to encounter as a living being rather than as an abstract doctrine or inherited symbol.

Yet this imagined closeness never fully resolves God’s disappearance. Instead, the search leads to a paradox: absence itself becomes the place where God is most powerfully concealed. The divine is encountered not through certainty or visible revelation, but through the speaker’s inability to stop looking. Longing keeps God present precisely as the one who cannot be found. The speaker’s restless attention to bodily experience, emotional need, and the limits of religious representation therefore becomes a form of faith. Belief does not take the shape of calm assurance; it appears as desire, questioning, and persistent direct address. By continuing to speak to an apparently absent God, the speaker treats that absence as meaningful rather than empty. Faith survives as the embodied act of seeking—a refusal to let silence, distance, or illusion bring the encounter to an end.
outputs.L5:
**See You, Gulf**

At sunset, the Gulf turns to silver, holding the last light like a promise. Waves reach softly for the shore, then slip away again.

You stand where the land ends, listening to seabirds and distant boats.

“See you,” you whisper—not as a farewell, but as a promise to return.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem in which the speaker addresses God backstage in a dark theater, wrestling with divine absence, embodiment, Catholic imagery, and the inadequacy of Greek and Roman ideas about flesh.
counterfactuals.output:
God, I have found You backstage, if this is finding: among the ropes and sandbags, the blind curtains breathing dust, the costumes emptied of their saints. The theater is dark. Out beyond the velvet, the seats wait like rows of shut mouths. No audience, no orchestra, no moon in the painted window. Only the red lamp above the exit, small as the vigil light before a tabernacle.

I address the darkness because it has Your posture.

Were You here before the house went black? Did You slip away during the final scene, while we were still praising the machinery of thunder? I heard the pulleys groan. I saw the papier-mâché rock split open. The actor playing Lazarus rose, took his applause, and afterward smoked beneath the fire escape with rouge still warming his dead cheeks.

You have always allowed us substitutes.

Incense for breath. Bells for astonishment. Gold leaf for the unendurable blaze. A wafer lifted in two trembling fingers while the body, that poor animal, kneels and hungers below. I was taught to strike my breast as if knocking on a locked door: through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault. But who is inside, God? Who keeps silent while the knuckles redden?

The Greeks gave flesh a bright grammar: proportion, marble, the athlete poised forever before sweat can sour him. The Romans made it law and spectacle—muscle under armor, bodies numbered, crucifixions efficient along the road. Neither knew enough of skin. Neither carved the bruise blooming beneath it, the fever’s wet linen, the milk leaking through a mother’s dress, the old man’s hand unable to lift the spoon. Their gods wore bodies as costumes. They entered shining and exited without scars.

But You—You are said to have entered badly: blood first, then hunger, then the long apprenticeship of touch. A mouth at a breast. Splinters in the palm. Mud between the toes. Spit. Tears. The belly’s emptiness. The body’s final, humiliating weight.

I want to believe this was not a metaphor.

Back here, the crucifix leans against a flatscreen heaven. Christ has been taken down between performances. One arm is wrapped in muslin; the crown of thorns hangs from a nail beside a janitor’s coat. His plaster wound is dark enough to enter. I put my finger there—not like Thomas, not bravely, but as a child touches a tear in the scenery and discovers no kingdom behind it, only brick, cold air, another wall.

Where are You when the body becomes unbearable?

Do not answer with Plato’s ladder. Do not send me upward from the beloved shoulder toward some bloodless form of Beauty. Do not teach me to despise the prison because I cannot survive its doors. If flesh is a cage, why did You ask for its key? Why sleep in the red cell of Mary? Why become an infant whose skull had not yet closed, Your infinity pulsing beneath a membrane thin as stage silk?

Mother of God, they called her, and painted her blue, though childbirth is red. They gave her lilies, though she must have smelled of iron, sweat, and animals. Even our tenderness edits the body. Even our icons clean the floor.

God, I am tired of clean salvation.

Come near in the greasepaint and damp wool, in the ache behind the knee, in the tooth loosening from its root. Be present in the hand that washes another body when love has become labor. Be the stubborn warmth that remains in the cup after the wine is gone. If the Host is flesh, let flesh be more than a door You passed through once. Let it be where You still consent to be wounded.

The stage manager has gone home. Somewhere a pipe ticks in the wall. I wait beside the hanging costumes: pope, beggar, soldier, angel. They sway though there is no wind.

Perhaps absence is the last mask You wear.

Perhaps I have mistaken silence for distance, darkness for an empty house. Perhaps You are not in the rafters but under my tongue, dissolving—small, tasteless, impossible to prove. Perhaps You are the hunger after communion, not its end.

Still, I speak.

God, if You are here, do not step into the light unchanged. Come limping. Come with dust on Your hem and the spear’s grammar broken in Your side. Come unable to explain why resurrection keeps the wounds. Stand with me behind the curtain while the world rehearses its dying.

And when at last the house lights rise, let us not be marble.

Let us be flesh: unfinished, afraid, radiant with damage—  
the body not escaped,  
but entered completely;  
the Word not above us,  
but warm in the mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental monologue about faith and doubt. Use lush Southern ecological imagery, references to the Gulf and bayou, Catholic sacramentals, and a final image of God hiding with knees drawn to the chest.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep my doubt in a blue Mason jar beneath the sink,  
beside the lye soap and the wasp-deadening kerosene.  
Some nights it gives off light. Not much—  
a foxfire shimmer, a swamp’s green whisper—  
but enough to silver the pipes, enough to make me kneel  
without knowing whether I am praying  
or only looking for a leak.

Faith was easier when the world smelled of beeswax:  
the church door sweating in August,  
the holy water cool as a coin on my forehead,  
Saint Christopher riding the dashboard through thunder,  
a rosary blooming from my grandmother’s fist.  
She believed each bead was a rung on a ladder.  
I believed because she did.  
Is that grace, or merely gravity?

Outside, the bayou turns its black pages.  
Cypress knees rise from the shallows  
like a congregation that has forgotten the words.  
Egrets lift their white vestments from the reeds.  
An alligator shuts one prehistoric eye.  
Spanish moss combs the wind for omens.

And south of us the Gulf keeps breathing—  
salt lung, oil-dark mirror,  
mother of hurricanes and mullet,  
dragging moonlight through its teeth.  
I ask it what survives.  
It answers by taking the shore.

At Mass, the bell rings once, twice, three times,  
and the bread becomes what the mouth cannot prove.  
Incense climbs in extravagant doubt.  
The priest raises the chalice;  
every mosquito in Louisiana continues its small blood liturgy.  
I taste iron. I taste rain. I say amen  
because amen may mean *yes*,  
or may mean *I have come this far*.

Do not tell me doubt is faith’s opposite.  
Doubt is faith’s wet hem,  
faith’s thumbprint on the locked tabernacle,  
faith walking barefoot at midnight  
where the levee grass hisses with snakes.  
I have doubted with all my body.  
I have believed with none of it.  
Still, I wear the scapular.  
Still, I strike the match.  
Still, I touch the medal at my throat  
when the wind begins naming the dead.

Perhaps heaven is not above us.  
Perhaps it is tangled in the roots—  
among crawfish chimneys, lost fishhooks,  
beer cans softened by mud,  
the drowned bells of vanished towns.  
Perhaps every sacramental is only a small door  
we press our faces against,  
hoping to feel warmth on the other side.

Tonight the Gulf is far off, but I hear it.  
The bayou holds the moon like a broken host.  
Frogs chant their blunt antiphon.  
My jar of doubt burns under the sink.

And somewhere beyond doctrine, beyond weather,  
beyond the last candle guttering in its red glass,  
I imagine opening the smallest door in creation  
and finding God hiding there,  
knees drawn to the chest.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, first-person prose poem addressed to “You,” where “You” is an absent God. Contrast theatrical scenery with a damaged landscape, then meditate on incarnation, apophatic theology, and the need for flesh not merely to die but to live.
counterfactuals.output: You, absent behind the fly-tower of heaven, have left the painted dawn trembling on its ropes: cardboard olive trees, a river of blue silk, one immaculate hill rolled forward for the final act. But I have walked beyond the footlights where the ground forgets its cues—orchards blistered to wire, wells gagged with rubble, the black grammar of roads shelled into parentheses—and no stagehand comes to mend the horizon. I call this world Your scenery until splinters enter my palm; then I call it wound. I call You Father, fire, breath, vacancy, knowing each name is another curtain lowered before what cannot enter speech. The theologians polish negation: not this, not that, neither being nor absence, a darkness brighter than knowledge. Yet I am tired of holy subtraction. If You are beyond every word, take up the word that bruises. If You are without image, borrow the face that hungers. Incarnation cannot be merely Your brief costume of blood, flesh tailored for execution, a body assumed so it may be broken with doctrinal precision. I need You born not only toward the nail but toward milk, sweat, sleep, fever, laughter—the long apprenticeship of touch. I need Your hands to learn the stubborn weight of bread, Your lungs to consent to ordinary air, Your feet to ache from carrying You through the damaged actual. Come live in what dies, yes, but also in what survives: the scar knitting badly, the child rehearsing tomorrow among ruins, the weed lifting its green refusal through the bombed proscenium. Otherwise the tomb is only another trapdoor, resurrection another trick of light, and I remain here, speaking into the wings, loving the silence because I have no proof it is not You.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the voice of a skeptical queer Catholic speaker who corners God offstage for an intimate confrontation. Make the tone irreverent yet aching, blending bodily gestures, religious artifacts, classical theology, and divine hide-and-seek.
counterfactuals.output:
**After Benediction, Behind the Curtain**

Don’t “mysterious ways” me.

Not tonight.

I have followed You past the incense and the gilt, past Saint Michael standing on Satan’s neck like he’s posing for a parish fundraiser, past the sacristy sink where Father rinses Your blood from the chalice with two brisk turns of the wrist.

And here You are.

Or here You aren’t—which is Your favorite way of being everywhere.

I corner You offstage, behind the velvet curtain, where the plaster saints keep their hollow backs to us. My rosary is wound around my fist. Not prayerfully. More like evidence.

Look at me.

No, really. Look.

You made the body, allegedly. Thumbed Adam out of mud, breathed into his mouth, called the whole damp arrangement good. Then You act scandalized when I arrive in one—hips, hunger, pulse, all of it—loving whom I love with the embarrassing sincerity of a candle refusing to go out.

The Church says You are simple.

*Divine simplicity.*

No parts. No passions. No change.

Must be nice.

I am all parts. I am a committee meeting in a locked room. I am knees bruised from kneeling and from other things the catechism declines to picture. I am a tongue trained to say *Lord, I am not worthy* while every nerve in me whispers, Then why did He come under my roof?

Aquinas says You are Being itself.

Fine.

Be here.

Not in the tabernacle with the little red lamp burning like an alibi. Not in the host—thin, white, obedient, impossible. Here. In this cramped dark where my collar is crooked and my hands smell of chrism and sweat. Here, where I can accuse You without the organ covering for me.

You hide like a lover who wants to be pursued but never touched.

Behind bread.

Behind doctrine.

Behind the face of every beautiful stranger, which is frankly cruel.

I have played Your game. I have found You in hospital elevators, in drag queens pinning each other’s wigs, in the old woman who presses a holy card into my palm as if slipping me cash. I have found You in the mouth of the man I loved when he said my name without apology.

Then Sunday comes, and someone reads Saint Paul like a warrant.

Where do You go then?

Do You duck behind the ambo? Crawl into the censer? Hold Your breath inside the priest?

I’m tired of defending You.

I’m tired of translating thunder into tenderness.

I’m tired of being told the locked door is mercy because someone carved a cross into it.

My thumb worries the crucifix until the little metal Christ digs into my skin. There. A mark. At least Your silence has edges.

If You are impassible, why the wounds?

If You are unchanging, why Easter?

If You need nothing, why make creatures who ache to be wanted by You?

Answer carefully.

I have brought all my heresies, and some of them are just grief wearing lipstick.

The curtain stirs.

No wind.

Of course.

That is so like You: the hem of a garment, the back of a head, a footprint cooling in the garden. Divine hide-and-seek, and somehow I am always “it.”

I should leave.

I should drop the beads, spit out the Creed, walk into the clean secular night.

Instead, traitorously, my hand opens.

The rosary slips loose between my fingers.

And in the dark—whether You touch me or I merely remember being touched—I feel something at my wrist: two fingers, light as absolution, taking my pulse.

I hate You for knowing exactly where to look.

I love You for looking.

There.

Now we’re both in trouble.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a single-paragraph literary passage beginning with “See, now You are finally offstage where we can talk.” Include drapes and pulleys, moss and oaks, a collapsing bayou, a monstrance, milagro, scapular, palm frond, household goddess, Greeks and Romans, and God’s heart beating in a corner.
counterfactuals.output: See, now You are finally offstage where we can talk. Behind the velvet drapes and patient pulleys, beyond the footlights dimming like drowned stars, the moss and oaks lean over a collapsing bayou, listening as the earth takes back its black water and ruined porches. Someone has left a monstrance gleaming on a crate beside a silver milagro, a frayed scapular, and a palm frond folded into a brittle cross; they look like props until the household goddess lifts her floury hands and blesses them. The Greeks and Romans would have recognized her, though they might have given her a marble face and a name fit for thunder, while here she keeps watch over cold coffee, bent spoons, and photographs curling in their frames. No audience remains, no chorus to explain what we have lost, only ropes creaking overhead and frogs calling from the dark, and God’s heart beating in a corner, small and stubborn as a moth trapped beneath a glass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
